Bio
James Jaxxa’s multi-faceted practice explores themes of memory, desire, vulnerability, community and pleasure through the creation of bedazzling personal reliquaries and cathartic shrines. His work is influenced from growing up nomadically in a military family, Catholic iconography and queer culture.

He received his MFA from the School of Visual Arts, his BS from Michigan State University and completed post-baccalaureate work at School of the Art Institute of Chicago and Rhode Island School of Design. He has attended residencies at Barac (Mannheim, Germany), Salzburg International Summer Academy (Salzburg, Austria), R.A.R.O. (Barcelona, Spain), Berlin Art Institute (Berlin, Germany) and others.

Jaxxa’s work has been shown in exhibitions across the United States and internationally including those at Terrain Biennial, New York Public Library, The LGBT Center in New York, University of Nevada, Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art, Seattle Art Museum, Bellevue Art Museum and numerous other institutions and galleries. His public artwork, Potential Connections was installed for the inauguration of Seattle’s Link Light Rail system. Jaxxa has been included in publications by The New York Times, Visual AIDS, New York Public Library and The Seattle Times. He was awarded an Artists Space Independent Project Grant.

Jaxxa is a founding member of I Found U, an international group of artists working across different materials and mediums, committed to discussion and collaboration on environmental, sociological and economic concerns. He lives and works in New York City.

event.title: Broadway Comes To Bradley II
event.description:
Broadway Comes To Bradley II
October, 3, 2026 at 7:30pm in the Meyer Jacobs Theatre

For one night only… Broadway performer and Bradley University Theatre Arts Performance alum Morgan Siobhan Green, along with award-winning composer and lyricist Joe Iconis, are coming to Bradley!

After last year’s triumphant Broadway Comes to Bradley, in which Morgan performed alongside Tony and Pulitzer Prize winner Michael R. Jackson (A Strange Loop), we are thrilled to bring Morgan back again, along with another of her dear friends from the world of Broadway: composer and lyricist Joe Iconis.

Morgan was one of Bradley Theatre’s all-time best actors, excelled on BU’s Speech Team, and performed in Broadway’s Be More Chill and in the US National Tour of the smash-hit Broadway musical Hadestown.

Joe’s highly acclaimed musical Be More Chill was nominated for numerous Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circle awards. This prolific artist has also written the music and lyrics for the musicals Broadway Bounty Hunter and Love in Hate Nation, and developed the musicals The Untitled Hunter S. Thompson Musical and Punk Rock Girl, among many other projects.

Morgan and Joe, along with Bradley’s Theatre Arts and Music students, will perform an evening of original music that is sure to delight and inspire.

Tickets can be purchased in-person at the Hartmann Center box office, or online.

Please join us for Broadway Comes to Bradley II – an exciting evening of music and fun!

event.title: BSides Peoria 2026
event.description:
Join the Illinois Cyber Foundation and the Center for Cybersecurity at Bradley University for BSides Peoria 2026, a one-day, community-driven cybersecurity conference bringing together professionals, students, educators, researchers and enthusiasts for a day of learning, hands-on exploration and collaboration.

Returning to Bradley on Saturday, Oct. 24, BSides Peoria features 15 technical talks, a dedicated keynote from Alethe Denis, hands-on villages, competitions and networking opportunities spanning a wide range of cybersecurity topics.

Attendees can explore the Physical Security Village, Human Hacking Village and Radio Frequency Village, with activities covering lockpicking and physical access controls, social engineering and human behavior, wireless technologies and RF security. Competitions include the BSides Peoria Capture the Flag, Vishing Challenge, Zero Trust, and Phish Bowl, offering opportunities for both experienced participants and newcomers to test their skills.

BSides events are built by the cybersecurity community, for the cybersecurity community, emphasizing accessible learning, conversation and participation. The Center for Cybersecurity has hosted BSides Peoria at Bradley University since the conference was established by the Illinois Cyber Foundation in 2023.

Whether you work in cybersecurity, are preparing to enter the field, or are simply curious about how technology can be attacked and defended, BSides Peoria offers opportunities to learn something new, meet others in the community and get hands-on with cybersecurity.

Registration is required. Visit BSidesPeoria.com for tickets, conference updates and additional information.

event.title: Henry IV, Part 1 by William Shakespeare
event.description:
Henry IV, Part 1 by William Shakespeare
November 5 – 15, 2026 in the O’Sullivan Studio Theatre
Directed by Debbie Alley

Bradley returns to the O’Sullivan Studio Theatre for a mainstage production for the first time since 2017 with Henry IV, Part One, a Shakespearean masterpiece about King Henry IV’s struggle with rebellious nobles (particularly Henry “Hotspur” Percy), while his son, Prince Hal, navigates a wild life with the roguish Falstaff, before proving his worth.

This history play, written around 1597, covers the period from late 1402 to mid-1403 and explores themes of honor, rebellion, and father-son relationships, contrasting the king’s disappointment in Hal with his envy of Hotspur’s gallantry. The production will be guest-directed by Debbie Alley, a nationally respected theatre artist and educator.

event.title: Eyewitness to History: Inside the Presidency with Pete Souza – Voices & Visionary Series
event.description:
Go behind the scenes of the presidency with Pete Souza as he shares iconic photos and stories from inside the White House.

Step inside the most powerful office in the world with renowned White House photographer Pete Souza.

As the only photographer to serve as Chief Official White House Photographer for both Presidents Barack Obama and Ronald Reagan, Souza offers a rare behind-the-scenes look at the presidency through the lens of his camera. Over decades in the White House, he captured defining moments of leadership, crisis, and humanity, many of which have become iconic images in modern American history.

In Eyewitness to History: Inside the Presidency, Souza shares unforgettable photographs and the stories behind them, offering a candid and deeply personal perspective on what it is really like to document history as it happens.

This special event is part of OLLI at Bradley University’s Voices and Visionaries series, bringing influential voices and extraordinary experiences to our community. Parking will be free on campus for all attendees.

Event Registration: Free

Bio
James Jaxxa’s multi-faceted practice explores themes of memory, desire, vulnerability, community and pleasure through the creation of bedazzling personal reliquaries and cathartic shrines. His work is influenced from growing up nomadically in a military family, Catholic iconography and queer culture.

He received his MFA from the School of Visual Arts, his BS from Michigan State University and completed post-baccalaureate work at School of the Art Institute of Chicago and Rhode Island School of Design. He has attended residencies at Barac (Mannheim, Germany), Salzburg International Summer Academy (Salzburg, Austria), R.A.R.O. (Barcelona, Spain), Berlin Art Institute (Berlin, Germany) and others.

Jaxxa’s work has been shown in exhibitions across the United States and internationally including those at Terrain Biennial, New York Public Library, The LGBT Center in New York, University of Nevada, Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art, Seattle Art Museum, Bellevue Art Museum and numerous other institutions and galleries. His public artwork, Potential Connections was installed for the inauguration of Seattle’s Link Light Rail system. Jaxxa has been included in publications by The New York Times, Visual AIDS, New York Public Library and The Seattle Times. He was awarded an Artists Space Independent Project Grant.

Jaxxa is a founding member of I Found U, an international group of artists working across different materials and mediums, committed to discussion and collaboration on environmental, sociological and economic concerns. He lives and works in New York City.

Saar’s work examines the place of the female body in the realms of politics and spirituality. Saar has exhibited artworks at many galleries and museums throughout the United States. Her 1997 piece, “Sweeping Beauty” was added to the Des Moines Art Center’s permanent collection in 2003.

event.title: Fright Night with Final Act Ensemble
event.description:
Welcome to Fright Night at the Art Center! The Des Moines Community Playhouse’s Final Act Ensemble brings ghosts, witches, murder, and mystery to life in a Halloween performance inspired by the golden age of radio.

The evening features three chilling tales: “The Woman Who Wouldn’t Die,” in which a man begins to suspect his wife may be a witch burned more than 200 years ago; a spooky story of stranded teenagers, a possible dead body, and a mysterious stranger; and “The Moonlit Road,” Ambrose Bierce’s classic tale about a man who discovers the terrifying truth behind his mother’s murder.

For nearly 20 years, the Final Act Ensemble—a company of older adult actors—has performed polished old-time radio shows throughout the Des Moines area. This production features live acting, music, and sound effects.

Free; no registration required. Run time: approximately 50 minutes.

Please note: This program may not be suitable for younger children. The stories include death, murder, supernatural themes, eerie music, and spooky sound effects. Although portions of the performance are humorous, some children may find the program frightening.

event.title: “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” Curator and Artist Discussion
event.description:
Join the Des Moines Art Center for an invigorating discussion about the traveling exhibition organized by the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way: Contemporary Latinx Painting,” which is on view at the Art Center from October 24, 2026, through January 24, 2027. Inspired by a 2008 poem of the same name by former US Poet Laureate Juan Felipe Herrera, “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” celebrates the vision and creativity of Latinx painters. It showcases 58 artists who actively enrich the landscape of contemporary painting, introducing new approaches to form, materials, and subject matter.

Dr. Andrea Alvarez, curator of the exhibition, will provide insight into the premise of the show and introduce us to three of the featured artists: Danielle De Jesus, Justin Favela, and Patrick Martinez.

REGISTER

Danielle De Jesus is a Nuyorican painter and photographer born and raised in Bushwick, Brooklyn, whose woks tell the story of growing up in New York City amid gentrification and displacement. De Jesus’s background is in photography, and she utilizes her images of people native to Bushwick as a reference to tell the story of the community’s displaced residents.

Justin Favela is based in Las Vegas and is known for large-scale installations and sculpture that manifest his interactions with American pop culture and the queer Latinx experience. Favela explores traditional Mexican and Latin American craft — specifically cartoneria (a traditional Mexican folk art form that involves three-dimensional objects using papier-mâché and cardboard) — and his interest in art history, community, celebration, and home inform a practice intent on dismantling institutional hierarchies. Visitors may remember Favela from his 2021 exhibition at the Art Center, “Central American.”

Patrick Martinez maintains a diverse practice that includes mixed-media landscape paintings, neon signs pieces, cake paintings, and his Pee Chee series of appropriative works. His landscape paintings composed of Los Angeles surfaces — distressed stucco, spray paint, window security bars, vinyl signage, ceramic tile, and neon sign elements — evoke place and socioeconomic positions, unearth sites of personal and cultural loss. He lives and works in Los Angeles.

Free; registration required.

REGISTER

event.title: Day of the Dead / Día de Los Muertos
event.description:
Day of the Dead 2026: ¡Sí Se Puede!

Join us for the 26th annual Día de los Muertos at the Des Moines Art Center—our largest community celebration of the year. Rooted in Mexican tradition, Día de los Muertos is a time to gather in remembrance, honoring loved ones who have died through joy, ritual, storytelling, food, art, and shared celebration. The Art Center is pleased to help create space for this meaningful community tradition each year.

This year’s theme centers on civil rights, inspired by the phrase ¡Sí Se Puede! (“Yes, we can”), created by Dolores Huerta for the United Farm Workers movement. Together, we honor the people and collective efforts that have strengthened Latino communities in Iowa and across the United States, while reflecting on the power of gathering, shared purpose, and community care.

Visitors will enjoy live music and dance performances, food and art vendors, hands-on art activities, a festive Catrina photo opportunity, a community ofrenda, and a short documentary film featuring this year’s honoree, Felicia Timotea Leon Mullin. Free hot cocoa and samples of pan de muerto will be available while supplies last, and a complimentary shuttle will run from Merrill Middle School for easy parking.

Inspired in part by the Art Center’s current exhibition “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way: Contemporary Latinx Painting,” this year’s event reflects gathering, belonging, and the ways communities care for one another. In partnership with Progress Iowa and other community organizations, we’ll also recognize local leadership and the collective work of building stronger communities.

At its heart, Día de los Muertos at the Art Center is about community. It’s a space where art, culture, memory, and shared tradition bring people together. The Des Moines Art Center is proud to be a welcoming and inspiring cultural space for all.

Take advantage of easy parking and a free shuttle from Merrill Middle School, running continuously from 11 am to 3 pm.

Con raíces en la tradición mexicana, el Día de los Muertos es un momento para reunirnos en conmemoración, rindiendo homenaje a nuestros seres queridos fallecidos a través de la alegría, los rituales, las narrativas, la comida, el arte y la celebración en comunidad. Para el Art Center es un honor ayudar a crear un espacio para esta importante tradición comunitaria cada año.

La temática de este año explora los derechos civiles, inspirada por la frase ¡Sí Se Puede!, creada por Dolores Huerta para el movimiento de la Unión de Campesinos (United Farm Workers). Juntos, honramos a las personas y los esfuerzos colectivos que han fortalecido a las comunidades latinas en Iowa y en todo Estados Unidos, reflexionando también en torno al poder de la concurrencia, un propósito común y el cariño por la comunidad.

Habrá música y presentaciones de baile en vivo para disfrutar, vendedores de comida y arte, actividades interactivas de arte, oportunidades para tomarse fotos festivas con el personaje de la Catrina, una ofrenda comunitaria y un breve documental en reconocimiento a Felicia Timotea Leon Mullin, la homenajeada de este año. Habrá chocolate caliente y pan de muerto gratis hasta agotarse la existencia; también tendremos transporte gratuito desde la escuela Merrill Middle School para estacionar con facilidad.

Inspirado, en parte, por la exhibición concurrente del Art Center, Reunámonos de manera esplendorosa (Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way), el evento de este año hará reflexión respecto a la concurrencia, la pertenencia y las maneras en que las comunidades demuestran cariño y se preocupan unas por otras. En colaboración con Progress Iowa y otras organizaciones comunitarias, también reconoceremos a líderes locales y su trabajo colectivo en la construcción de comunidades más fuertes.

En esencia, el Día de los Muertos en el Art Center se trata de nuestra comunidad. Es un espacio donde el arte, la cultura, los recuerdos y la tradición compartida unen a las personas. El Des Moines Art Center se enorgullece de ser un espacio cultural de bienvenida e inspiración para todas las personas.

event.title: Honoring the Spirit: A Day of the Dead Ofrenda Conversation
event.description:
Join the Des Moines Art Center for an exploration of what it means to honor the spirit — of loved ones, of cultural traditions, and of movements that have advanced justice and strengthened our communities.

At the center of the conversation is this year’s Day of the Dead ofrenda, created by poet and artist Michaela Mullin, in honor of her mother, Felicia Leon Mullin, and alongside local organizations which are continuing to advance the quality of life for all Iowans. Through the ofrenda and this year’s theme, Sí Se Puede!, panelists will consider how we remember those who have contributed to civil and human rights work, how their values live on through the people and communities they influenced, and why this work remains urgent today.

Opening with a brief Know Your Rights presentation led by Karina Sanchez of the Des Moines Civil and Human Rights Commission, this program will feature a conversation with Mullin; Vince Valdez, historian, filmmaker, and longstanding Day of the Dead committee member; and Erica Johnson, the founding Executive Director of Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Art Center Senior Manager of Museum Learning and Engagement, Mia Buch, will moderate. Join us for an inspiring conversation about remembrance, immigrant rights, community action, and carrying the work of previous generations forward.

Free; no registration required.

event.title: A Taste of ReelAbilities
event.description:
The ReelAbilities Film Festival is the largest festival in the US dedicated to promoting awareness and appreciation of the lives, stories, and artistic expressions of people with disabilities. Founded in New York City in 2007, the festival presents international and award-winning films by and about people with disabilities in multiple locations throughout each hosting city. The 2026 Des Moines festival, “A Taste of ReelAbilities,” is a screening of recent short films during the Art Center’s November Social Saturday: Friendsgiving. All films will provide open captions and have audio description capabilities.

Generous support provided by Art Bridges Foundation’s Access for All program.

Free; no registration required.

Screening Information:
Film: A Morning with Aroha, 2021
Director: Nicholas Rini
Run Time: 11 minutes
Description: Aroha, an imaginative young girl with Down syndrome, sets out to share her creativity with her neighbors.

Film: Key of Genius, 2026
Director: Daniel Persitz
Run Time: 12 minutes
Description: Based on the extraordinary true story of Derek Paravicini, a blind, autistic musical prodigy, KEY OF GENIUS follows the bond between Derek and his dedicated piano teacher. Through patience, intuition, and unwavering belief, Derek’s hidden potential is unlocked, revealing the transformative power of music and mentorship. This film celebrates talent, perseverance, and the ways people with disabilities can flourish when given opportunity and understanding. Audiences are invited into a journey of inspiration, emotional depth, and triumph, witnessing a remarkable story of human connection, creativity, and the extraordinary capabilities that lie within those societies often underestimated.

*The following films are intended for adult audiences.

Film: Boys, 2026
Director: Olive Bilic
Run Time: 7 minutes
Description: Overwhelmed by the chaos of class, neurodiverse teenager Jacob seeks refuge in an empty locker room, only to face an unexpected confrontation. Created in collaboration with Bus Stop Films participants in Melbourne, BOYS highlights the emotional and social challenges faced by neurodiverse youth. Through authentic performances and an intimate lens, the film portrays the tension, vulnerability, and resilience of its characters, exploring the fine line between isolation and connection. BOYS is both a poignant and engaging narrative, offering insight into neurodiverse experiences while emphasizing the universal desire for understanding, acceptance, and human connection.

Film: Little Monsters, 2026
Director: Pablo Leridon
Run Time: 14 minutes
Description: A visually impaired teen navigates first love while sharing a transport van with a wheelchair-bound classmate. LITTLE MONSTERS blends humor and heart, showcasing adolescence, rivalry, and inclusive friendship.

Film: Bad Survivor, 2026
Director: Alex Dvorak and Katie North
Run Time: 11 minutes
Description: After being “broken up with” by her oncologists, a sarcastic young cancer patient begins her first day in remission, navigating the challenges of returning home. With humor and biting honesty, she confronts her family dynamics, cultural expectations, and the lingering trauma of treatment. BAD SURVIVOR balances comedy and pathos, portraying survival not as a singular triumph but as a process filled with awkward moments, personal reflection, and familial tension. Audiences are drawn into an intimate portrait of post-cancer life, where resilience, wit, and emotional vulnerability coexist, redefining what it means to move forward after illness.

Film: Don’t Take this the Wrong Way, 2026
Director: Rachel Handler and Crystal Arnette
Run Time: 7 minutes
Description: Darcy, beaten down by microaggressions and a recent breakup, begins to unravel emotionally. DON’T TAKE THIS THE WRONG WAY presents a raw exploration of personal vulnerability, societal pressures, and coping with isolation. The short captures moments of introspection, tension, and resilience, offering audiences an intimate glimpse into the lived experience of an amputee navigating social and emotional challenges. Through concise storytelling and authentic performances, the film conveys the complexity of identity, self-esteem, and the subtle ways everyday interactions can shape one’s emotional landscape.

Film: Misfit, 2026
Director: Tristan Zerbib
Run Time: 13 minutes
Description: In a world where disability is the norm, wheelchair-ball dominates the sports scene. A player is thrown off balance when forced to train with a ‘valid’ athlete, challenging her expectations and assumptions. MISFIT turns conventional sports narratives upside down, celebrating empowerment, inclusion, and the unpredictability of competition. Through fast-paced action and engaging character work, the film explores societal perceptions of ability and the courage required to embrace difference. MISFIT is a bold, energetic story that champions physical resilience, adaptability, and teamwork while entertaining audiences with humor, tension, and the triumph of spirit.

Film: Rearranged, 2025
Director: Liz Whitmere
Run Time: 12 minutes
Description: Set within the intimate confines of a hospice, REARRANGED explores how irritation, vulnerability, and humor can unexpectedly give way to human connection. Led by blind actor Bruce Horak, the film challenges assumptions about care, agency, and intimacy, revealing how small disruptions can reshape relationships.

Film: Them That’s Not, 2025
Director: Mekhai Lee
Run Time: 19 minutes
Description: Andrea “Drea” Stoney, a Deaf poet, attends her grandmother’s repass and navigates a family that doesn’t understand ASL. Complicating matters, her father is temporarily released from prison for the day, forcing Drea to reconcile with him amid grief. THEM THAT’S NOT explores identity, communication, and familial tension, highlighting the challenges Deaf individuals face within hearing-centered spaces. Through introspection, subtle humor, and emotional honesty, the film portrays the resilience required to carve personal space and connection, offering audiences insight into Deaf culture, intergenerational dynamics, and the quiet power of language, love, and understanding.

event.description:
In recognition of World AIDS Day, join us at the Des Moines Art Center for A Day With(out) Art — a day to come together using art, film, and music as a space for healing, remembrance, and hope. Founded in 1989 at the Museum of Modern Art, this event is a call to action, care, and reflection on AIDS’ impact. event.title: Art + Car Culture from a Rat Fink Artist- October Tread Talk
event.description:
Get ready to dive into the colorful and creative world of Rat Fink and Kustom Kulture with artist Dan-O!
Inspired by legendary artist Ed “Big Daddy” Roth and the Kustom Kulture scene, Dan-O has been creating art since elementary school. During this special Tread Talk, he’ll share his journey as an artist, what inspired him to become a Rat Fink artist, and the history behind the Kustom Kulture movement.
Dan-O’s artwork has been featured in magazines, books and coloring books, and he currently has 36 pieces in the Rat Fink Museum. He’ll also bring along some of his artwork and share stories about his experiences as an artist in the car show world.
Whether you’re a longtime Rat Fink fan, an admirer of Kustom Kulture, or simply interested in the connection between cars and art, this is a Tread Talk you won’t want to miss!

event.title: Exhibition on Screen: James McNeill Whistler at Speed Cinema
event.description:
Exhibition on Screen: James McNeill Whistler
Directed by David Bickerstaff

Saturday, October 3, 12:30 pm CINEMA + | BUY TICKETS

$14 | $10 Speed members

In an era of great change and great beauty emerged the character of James McNeill Whistler. Considered by some to be one of the great innovators of 19th century art, he was a contemporary of the Impressionists, much admired by Vincent Van Gogh and Édouard Manet. Boldly experimental and famously witty, Whistler disrupted the strict conventions of Victorian society in pursuit of a new cult of beauty, creating “art for art’s sake” and earning himself a place in the history of great art. He found a parallel between painting and music, and entitled many of his paintings “arrangements,” “harmonies,” and “nocturnes,” emphasizing the importance of tonal unity in his work.

His most famous painting, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871), commonly known as Whistler’s Mother, is a revered and often parodied portrait of motherhood. It is arguably one of the most famous paintings in history, and this film will unveil the artist behind the art.

Tate Britain is now holding the first major retrospective of Whistler in three decades. This blockbuster exhibition promises to reawaken the world to just how important Whistler is to art history, uniting world-famous masterpieces with rarely seen works. This will be an unmissable chance to get to know this visually spectacular artist and the influence he has had on those who followed. 2027, U.K. DCP, 90 minutes. Recommended for 12+

CINEMA + with a post-screening opportunity to view a selection of the Speed’s 90+ works by Whistler on paper selected and presented by Kim Spence, Senior Director of Collections and Curator of Works on Paper

event.title: The History of Concrete at Speed Cinema
event.description:
The History of Concrete
Directed by John Wilson

Friday, October 9, 6 pm | BUY TICKETS

$12 | $8 Speed members

“Wilson’s debut feature The History of Concrete shows the expert essayist as sneakily profound as ever, contemplating life and art and piecing together meaning from the fragments.”—Nicolas Rapold, Sight & Sound

Following the finale of his acclaimed HBO series How To with John Wilson, NYC documentarian John Wilson looks to the bedrock of his beloved New York City for inspiration and structure. Concrete, the world’s most widely used building material, appears as an ever-present life force, and John sets out to make the definitive documentary on the matter. After attending a workshop on how to write and sell a Hallmark movie, he decides to use the industry-approved Hallmark formula to tell this seemingly drab story and increase his movie’s appeal. But his foundation soon begins to crumble—literally and figuratively—as he struggles to balance artistic freedom with the realities of the modern film industry. 2026, U.S., DCP, 100 minutes. Recommended for 16+

event.description:
Speed Together: Explore + Create 

REGISTER

A monthly Sunday of art, creativity, and self-guided discovery
Speed Together is a free Sunday program that focuses on ART, both looking at and making. This program offers the opportunity for families, friends, and first-time visitors to enjoy the galleries at their own pace, take advantage of Docent supported learning, or experiment with art materials in our open studios. Look for our welcome table near the Atrium to see what’s happening. 

Art in the Atrium, 1 – 4 PM 

Visitors of all ages are invited to make art in our light filled Atrium. Tables are stocked with the materials you’ll need to create your own work of art inspired by an artist or artwork in the museum. Accessible instructions are provided and a member of our creative making team is available to support. If you prefer to experiment and make your own thing, be sure to visit our open studio in Art Sparks, or try out both art experiences. 

Open Studio, 2 – 4 PM in the Prototype Lab (Art Sparks) 
A flexible, drop-in studio experience designed for independent exploration and creative play. Open Studio offers a self-guided environment with accessible materials, optional art prompts, and space to experiment freely, no instruction, no pressure. Whether you’re inspired after exploring the museum, continuing a project, trying something new, or simply looking for a quiet moment of making, our classroom becomes your space to explore, reflect, and create at your own rhythm. All ages are welcome. 

Special Programming:  
Join the Speed Art Museum for a special Speed Together: Explore + Create program in partnership with Center for Women and Families in observance of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. In addition to Art in the Atrium, traveling artist and muralist Jaylin Stewart will lead a hands-on art-making experience in Gheens court, inviting visitors of all ages to create, connect, and engage through art. Storytime with docents will also be available in Art Sparks from 2 –4 PM. This special programming is brought to you by funding support from Kentucky Foundation for Women. 

 

Partner Links: Center For Women & Families | Take Action for Safety Today

Focus: Mosaics
Legacy Workshops is a new creative series for adults ages 60 and older that invites participants to explore art making, connect with others, and honor the magic of a creative practice.
Join us this month as we focus on mosaic making! Explore color, pattern, and texture as you create your own mosaic at your own pace. We will have materials and guidance available, whether you’re new to mosaics or looking to experiment. As always, feel free to bring in past legacy workshop projects that you are working on. Create, explore, and spend time making art alongside others.
Bio: Stephen Batiz is a self-taught painter, illustrator, and installation artist exploring the spaces between isolation and connection. Through painting, drawing, and interactive experiences, he creates work that invites people to slow down, participate, and reflect on their own presence in the world. Rooted in curiosity and experimentation, Batiz’s practice transforms personal symbolism and material exploration into shared moments of recognition and connection.
Learn more about the artist: www.stephenbatiz.com

event.title: Speed Slow Down: Mama + Baby Flow
event.description:
Mama + Baby Flow with Encircle Movement, a part of Speed Slow Down: Rest + Restore

10am – 11:30am

REGISTER

A slow, grounded movement class for you and your baby. Expect mostly floor-based movement, with some standing poses you can do while holding your baby. We’ll open the hips, shoulders, and spine, ease tension from feeding and carrying, and make space for breath, rest, and connection.

Your baby is welcome exactly as they are; crying, feeding, napping, or needing to be held. Step away and come back whenever you need. Designed for newborns and pre-mobile babies, with all props provided. Wear comfortable clothes, bring a water bottle and anything you and baby need to be comfortable. Stay for light snacks, tea/coffee, and conversation. Restrooms with changing stations are nearby, a dedicated and private nursing room is onsite, and the museum is stroller accessible.

Come tired, come late, come as you are.

Your ticket includes gallery access because it’s never too early to introduce your baby to art! Galleries are stroller accessible, see a gallery attendant for help.

event.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall at Speed Cinema
event.description:
Music + Film/Presented in 35mm

Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall
Directed by Paul Thomas Anderson

Friday, December 18, 6 pm | BUY TICKETS

$12 | $8 Speed and LPM members 

On December 11, 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, Cameron Winter returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie.

Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (One Battle After Another), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (The Smashing Machine) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele).

GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has a “a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, Paste and Mojo and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker, NME, and Stereogum. A Janus Films and Criterion Release. 2026, U.S., 35mm, 72 minutes.

Co-presented with WFPK.

event.title: Garden & Estate Insider: Oak Hill Garden Walk
event.description:
Take a walk with Jessica Tsakiris, horticulturist, to visit this garden area and learn about its history as well as current plants and projects. Included with admission. Members free.

Register now.

Join our staff and invited experts as they share insights and information about Winterthur’s history, horticulture, or habitats. Activities may include a walk, talk, or demonstration and take place every Wednesday, April–October. 

Photo by Moonloop Photography

event.title: Introduction to T’ai Chi Chih
event.description:
Exclusively for Members! This introductory level, easy-to-learn set of twenty movements helps dissolve tension, reduce chronic pain, and improve balance. Based on the ancient Chinese principles of activation and circulation of energy (chi), T’ai Chi Chih is an easily adaptive and enjoyable program that can be done by anyone, regardless of age or physical ability. Classes are led by Jessica Lewis, accredited T’ai Chi Chih instructor. Classes meet outside the Picnic House in the rear of the Visitor Parking Lot and take place in the garden, weather permitting. In inclement weather, location will move indoors. Members only. $135. Registration is for all eight sessions. Capacity limited. Register by September 15. No class on October 22.

Register now.

event.title: Wellness Yoga
event.description:
Activate your internal energy and strengthen your body and spirit as you practice slow, easy motions to get into the rhythm of nature. Led by Beth Sheehy. Bring a yoga mat, small towel, and a water bottle. Wear layers appropriate to the season.

Drop-in classes; held in the garden, weather permitting. In inclement weather, location will move indoors. Locations will be posted by the main gate and outside Brown Horticulture Center. Members only. $15 per Member per class; cash only. For more information, contact Beth Sheehy at emsheehy@yahoo.com.

event.title: Story Time in Enchanted Woods
event.description:
Share the joy of reading while cultivating children’s interest in and appreciation for nature. Kids ages 3–6 sit among the Story Stones to hear nature-based stories. Plus, enjoy a special activity on the first Thursday of every month. Included with admission. Free for children under 2. Members free. Story Time starts promptly at scheduled time and takes place weekly, April–October.

October 1—Don’t Rake the Garden in a Party Dress by Aimee Bissonetti

October 8—Acorn Was a Little Wild by Jen Arena

October 15—Run Wild by David Covell

October 22—Daylight Starlight Wildlife by Wendell Minor

October 29—Animals in Winter by Henrietta Bancroft and Richard G. Van Gelder

Photo by Rob Cardillo

event.title: Winterthur in the Time of Jackie Kennedy Virtual Lecture
event.description:
Exclusively for Members! In this virtual lecture, walk in the footsteps of visitors to the museum and garden in the 1950s and ’60s, which included everyone from schoolchildren to America’s First Lady. In celebration of our 75th anniversary, Jeff Groff, former estate historian, will reveal Winterthur during its early years as a museum and explore how it was further transformed after H. F. du Pont’s death in 1969. Lecture followed by Q&A. Registration required. Free.

Register now.

event.title: Curator Talk: At Work at Winterthur
event.description:
Join Jennifer Vess, Winterthur archivist and curator of At Work at Winterthur, for a talk about the exhibition and to see a few items that didn’t make the final cut. 

Register now.

Photo from the Winterthur Archives

event.title: Harvest Hoedown: Line Dancing Party
event.description:
Step into fall with a night of line dancing, seasonal beverages, and tasty autumn treats. Learn new moves from our line dancing instructors, enjoy games on the lawn, and relax on hay bales under the crisp autumn sky. $50; $12 for children 12 and under. Includes welcome cocktail (nonalcoholic option available), line dancing instruction, and access to the garden. Rain date October 3.

Register now.

event.title: Truck & Tractor Day
event.description:
Get up close to big equipment, suit up in firefighter gear, take a hayride, and more on this day of farm-style fun. Included with admission. Members free. This is a rain or shine, drop-in event, although you may register in advance. 

Register now.

Photos by Suchat Pederson and Bob Leitch

Activate your internal energy and strengthen your body and spirit as you practice slow, easy motions to get into the rhythm of nature. Led by Beth Sheehy. Bring a yoga mat, small towel, and a water bottle. Wear layers appropriate to the season.

Drop-in classes; held in the garden, weather permitting. In inclement weather, location will move indoors. Locations will be posted by the main gate and outside Brown Horticulture Center. Members only. $15 per Member per class; cash only. For more information, contact Beth Sheehy at emsheehy@yahoo.com.

event.title: Off the Shelf: Marginalia
event.description:
Notes, doodles, little pointing hands…people of the past weren’t shy about marking in their books, and historians appreciate it! Join us to learn about the history and importance of marginalia and see some examples of the art from the library’s collections. Free. Reservations required; limited to 30 participants.

Register now.

event.title: Member Bloom Report Guided Garden Walk
event.description:
Exclusively for Members! Discover the beauty of the early fall garden on a walking tour led by Collin Hadsell, lead horticulturist. See what’s in bloom and explore unseen or off-the-beaten-path areas of the garden. Members free. Reservations required; limited to 50 participants. Walks leave promptly from the Visitor Center unless otherwise noted. In case of inclement weather, a decision will be made the day prior. If the decision is made to cancel, all registered participants will be notified.

Register now.

event.title: IRUG16: 16th Conference and Workshop of the Infrared and Raman User’s Group
event.description: For over three decades, the Infrared and Raman Users Group (IRUG) has been at the forefront of advancing spectroscopic analysis in cultural heritage conservation. Every few years, this vibrant international community gathers to share groundbreaking research, innovative techniques, and the latest developments in infrared and Raman spectroscopy for the analysis and conservation of cultural materials. In October 2026, IRUG 16 will bring together an international cohort of conservation scientists, conservators, researchers, and industry specialists working across diverse collections. This conference will showcase cutting-edge research and methodologies that are essential for advancing our understanding and preservation of cultural heritage materials.

event.title: Birding Walk
event.description:
Join us to explore some of the hotspots for birds at Winterthur, including wetlands, meadows, and the woodlands along Clenny Run. Observe resident birds as well as migrating raptors, warblers, and sparrows. For beginning or experienced bird watchers. Bring your binoculars. Be sure to dress for the weather and wear walking shoes. $20; $10 for Members. Park in the Visitor Parking Lot and meet at the Picnic House (the small building at the far end of the lot). Walks start promptly at scheduled time. In case of inclement weather, an update message will be left at 302.888.4864 by 7:00 am on the morning of the walk. Come prepared for a long walk.

Register now.

Additional Birding Walks take place on October 31 and November 11.

Photo by Eileen Tercha

event.title: Spectroscopy as Cultural Heritage
event.description:
Dr. Roger Turner will present a talk highlighting the fascinating history of cultural practices and social groups on the field of spectroscopy, the scientific study of how matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation. His talk introduces some of the hidden figures who helped make spectroscopy a powerful technique that scientists use to understand the compositions of cultural heritage objects—including paintings, textiles, archeological artifacts, photographs, contemporary art, and much, much more. Women like Clara Smith Craver created the books of chemical “fingerprints” that identify different materials, while groups of scientists learned to how to do spectroscopy through summer courses at Fisk University, a historically Black university. Surprising objects from the Science History Institute museum reveal that spectroscopists can be playful and silly, while doing work that has transformed our understanding of art and archeology. Dr. Turner is the curator of instruments and artifacts at the Science History Institute in Philadelphia.

This is the keynote lecture for the IRUG Conference taking place at Winterthur October 7–9. IRUG is a group dedicated to the use of infrared and Raman spectroscopies applied to cultural heritage. Included with admission. Members free.

event.description:
Join conservators and conservation graduate students from the Winterthur/University of Delaware Program in Art Conservation for a hands-on workshop about how to care for your cherished objects in hazardous flood conditions. Participants will have the opportunity to learn a variety of processes from freezing and drying books to safely removing heavy, wet textiles from flood waters.

event.title: Objects Up Close Virtual Series
event.description:
Portrait of Catherine de Visme Browne

When Henry Francis du Pont purchased this portrait and installed it prominently in Montmorenci Stair Hall, it was identified simply as an “American Empire Portrait.” Yet it is not a mere likeness. This portrait of Catherine de Visme Browne by Ezra Ames depicts a young woman of great intellect, beauty, and ability, and also presents an embodiment of taste and moral character within the cultural aspirations of the nation. It offers an authoritative statement—first for the Browne family and later for du Pont—about cultural refinement and aspiration, as expressed through material depictions. The talk is presented by Kayleigh Danowski, Lois F. McNeil Fellow, Winterthur Program in American Material Culture. Registration required. Free.

Register now.

event.title: Research at Winterthur Speaker Series
event.description:
A Nation Unraveled

During the American Civil War, clothing became central to the ways people waged war and experienced its cost. Through the clothes they made, wore, mended, lost, and stole, Americans expressed their allegiances, showed their love, confronted their social and economic challenges, subverted expectations, and, ultimately, preserved their history. As the collections they left behind make clear, Civil War Americans believed clothing was not merely a reflection of one’s class, gender, race, military rank, political ideology, or taste. Instead, Northerners and Southerners alike understood that clothing—from the weave of a fabric to the style and make of a coat—had the power to affect people’s way of living through the war’s tumult. In this lecture, Sarah Jones Weicksel discusses her new book, A Nation Unraveled: Clothing, Culture, and Violence in the American Civil War Era (University of North Carolina Press), a material history of war.  

The Research at Winterthur series, presented by the Library, Research Fellowship Program, and Continuing Education, showcases new projects and publications that tap into our rich collections and resources, unveiling innovative perspectives for exploring the fascinating stories that objects can tell about people and our shared past. Registration required. Included with admission. Members free. Lecture followed by book signing.

Register now.
